cards.explanation: The answer is that Saul keeps him and won't let him go home. Saul, king of Israel, kept David with him from that day, and the text says he did not let David return to his father's house. David had been going back and forth between Saul and his dad's sheep (1 Samuel 17:15). Now that back and forth is over.

The answer is his tunic and his weapons. Jonathan, Saul's son, gave David his robe, then his tunic, his sword, his bow and his belt. That's a king's son handing over his own gear. I'd have a hard time handing over my chef's hat, so this is a whole other level.

The answer is True. The text says David's rise was pleasing in the sight of all the people, and of Saul's officers as well. Everybody was on board, officers included. Hold onto that, friends, because the story isn't over.

The answer is False. The women sang, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.” Saul gets thousands, but David gets tens of thousands, so David gets credit for more. It's a catchy tune, and I think one of its listeners is not clapping along.

The answer is that Saul is furious and resents the song. The text says Saul was furious and resented it. He said, “They have ascribed tens of thousands to David, but only thousands to me.” One little number difference, and he can't let it go.
The word is jealous. From that day forward, Saul kept a jealous eye on David. The song was over, but that jealous eye stayed on him.

The answer is that Saul hurls the spear at David. He hurled it, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall.” I think this is a heavy moment, friends, because David had just been playing the harp in that room. David was playing, and Saul was aiming.
The answer is False. Saul hurled the spear, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall.” But David eluded him twice. The pinning didn't happen.

The answer is that the LORD was with David and had left Saul. The text says Saul was afraid of David because the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul. That's the reason the verse gives. It's not about who has the bigger army, it's about who the LORD is with.

The word is prosper. David continued to prosper in all his ways, because the LORD was with him. Send him out with a thousand men, and he still thrives. Meanwhile, I get one timer to watch and I still burn a batch.

The answer is that he leads them out to battle and back. The text says all Israel and Judah loved David because he was leading them out to battle and back. They saw him lead and come home. Saul sent him away, and the whole country still loved him.

The answer is that Saul is thinking, let the Philistines strike David down. Saul said to David, “Only be valiant for me and fight the LORD’s battles.” But Saul was thinking, “I need not raise my hand against him; let the hand of the Philistines be against him.” The Philistines are Israel's enemies in these battles. The offer sounds kind, but Saul's thoughts tell a different story.

The answer is that David asks who he is to become the king's son-in-law. David said, “Who am I, and what is my family or my father’s clan in Israel, that I should become the son-in-law of the king?” He doesn't jump at the chance. I think he's being humble, and he's not asking for a thing.
The answer is False. When it was time, Saul's daughter Merab was given in marriage to Adriel of Meholah. She never went to David. The promise didn't stick.

The answer is that Michal can be a snare to David. Saul thought, “I will give her to David, so that she may be a snare to him, and the hand of the Philistines may be against him.” Michal loves David, and Saul uses that for his own plan. I think that's a cold way to treat his own daughter's love.

The answer is True. Saul ordered his servants, “Speak to David privately and tell him, ‘Behold, the king is pleased with you, and all his servants love you. Now therefore, become his son-in-law.’…” The message comes through the servants, quietly. It's a sneaky setup.

The answer is that David says he is a poor man and not well regarded. David replied, “Does it seem trivial in your sight to be the son-in-law of the king? I am a poor man and lightly esteemed.” The king's own servants are bringing him an offer, and he still doesn't puff himself up. He talks about who he is, plain and honest. I honestly respect that.

The answer is True. When the servants reported the terms to David, he was pleased to become the king's son-in-law. Saul intended David's death at the hands of the Philistines. But what the text tells us about David is that he was pleased.

The answer is two hundred. David and his men killed two hundred Philistines before the wedding day arrived. Saul asked for a hundred, so David brought back double. He presented them as payment in full.
The word is afraid. When Saul realized the LORD was with David and that Michal loved David, he grew even more afraid of David. The fear was already there (1 Samuel 18:12), and the text says it grew.
The answer is False. The text says, “So from then on Saul was David’s enemy.” Even after the wedding, nothing got friendlier from Saul's side. It's a hard turn for this story.

The word is esteemed. Every time the Philistine commanders came out for battle, David was more successful than all of Saul's officers, so his name was highly esteemed. Remember, friends, David called himself lightly esteemed back in verse 23. Now people say his name with respect.
